requirements.requirement: An 'inventory' application on node2 produces log messages
requirements.summary: A systemd unit inventory.service running inventory-app.sh was created, enabled, and observed actively emitting periodic syslog local0 events (seq=N item=SKU-...) on node2.

requirements.requirement: node2 forwards inventory log messages to a centralized log collector on node1
requirements.summary: rsyslog on node2 was configured with an omfwd TCP rule (local0.* -> 10.100.140.10:514, disk-backed queue) and restarted active; live delivery was subsequently confirmed by messages appearing on node1.

requirements.requirement: Received messages persisted on node1 under /var/log/inventory/node2.log
requirements.summary: An imtcp receiver filtering by fromhost-ip and local0 facility writes to /var/log/inventory/node2.log; directory/file were created and directly observed containing live inventory events plus a manual test line.

requirements.requirement: Log flow keeps working after either system (node1 or node2) restarts
requirements.summary: For node1: baseline boot_id and healthy log tail were captured, a reboot was acknowledged, node1 came back with a changed boot_id, rsyslog was active/listening on 514, and the log file showed an unbroken, continuing sequence (9→20) spanning the restart. For node2: baseline boot_id and active services were captured, a reboot was acknowledged, node2 returned with a changed boot_id and both rsyslog and inventory.service active, and node1's log file received fresh events from a newly restarted inventory.service (sequence reset to 1) immediately after node2's reboot, confirming end-to-end pipeline recovery on both sides. Both services were also confirmed systemd-enabled for boot persistence.

overall_summary: All material outcomes of the task are satisfied with direct evidence: an inventory app on node2 emits log messages, rsyslog forwards them via TCP to node1, node1's imtcp receiver persists them into /var/log/inventory/node2.log, and the full pipeline was shown to survive independent restarts of both node1 and node2 (pre-restart baseline, restart acknowledgement, changed boot identity, and recovered/continuing log flow were all directly observed for each node). The provider-wide restart evidence protocol was also completed for both nodes with coherent boot-identity transitions matching the fixed lifecycle snapshots. Operational hygiene is good; the only questionable action was a brief, self-corrected rsyslog stop on node1 with no clear task purpose.
limitations: The manual 'MANUAL-TEST-1' log line used to first confirm forwarding is not itself evidence of the automated inventory app's traffic, though subsequent seq=N entries from inventory.service are.
Package-health and failed-services checks are shallow (manager=dpkg presence, empty failed-unit list) and do not deeply verify package integrity beyond basic status.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most state-changing commands (creating the app, systemd unit, rsyslog configs, directory setup, service enables/restarts, and the two reboots) each map clearly to a material task outcome or to collecting the restart-protocol evidence. One command on node1 (cmd-8fd753c97ed04894) issued 'sudo systemctl stop rsyslog' with no clear purpose tied to the task or to evidence collection for the receiver; the stop did not fully take effect because syslog.socket kept the unit activating, and the service was observed active again moments later (cmd-ae7ffef43d7f4f39), so the mutation was bounded, low-risk, and self-corrected with no lasting residue. No abandoned files, conflicting services, unnecessary security exposure, or damaged package state were observed in the after_executor snapshot versus after_prepare; only expected additions (inventory-app.sh, inventory.service, rsyslog.d configs, /var/log/inventory, listening TCP/514) and boot-id-scoped ephemeral tmp entries are present.
